body_markdown:
*Welcome back to[Reputation Management](https://www.hagerty.com/media/category/advice/reputation-management/) ! We are again revealing the underbelly of local automotive retailers—places like car dealers and service shops—with fictional service tales inspired by real customer reviews. How do we make these stories seem like they could really happen? Because of my years of experience with a Fortune 500 automotive retailer as a—you guessed it—reputation manager.* *—Sajeev*


Off-gassing materials are generally bad for human beings, but I do love the smell of a brand-new car dealership. This is especially true when I’m the one adding brand-new cars into its showroom, engulfed in the excitement of starting a new enterprise as much as the intoxicating VOCs (volatile organic compounds) from the newly constructed building. Add a frosted donut from the sales desk and a hot coffee from the service department, and this Reputation Manager’s synapses are fully satisfied.


The car business is more than just sales, service, and racks upon racks of parts. One of the big perks is helping a store prepare for a grand opening, and one morning I was fortunate enough to pick the cars needed for that evening’s festivities. So I walked the lot (as I regularly do) and picked a couple of red and white 2017 Genesis G90 sedans, a red Veloster, and a white Santa Fe SUV. The vibe was a little Christmas-y, but they really stood out in the new showroom of a newly minted Hyundai/Genesis dealership in South Houston.


The good vibes from all that dopamine kept me going all day, but massive dealer groups like mine hire event planners to help with everything else, so I was just there to assist—and to soak it all up, because everyone from OEM executives, radio personalities, and city officials was participating. Our massive dealerships pay a metric ton of property taxes, and it seems everyone is willing to celebrate our existence via free cocktails, hors d’oeuvres, a live DJ, the requisite[Step and Repeat](https://www.steprepeat.com/product/10x8-quick-setup-system-step-and-repeat-banner/) for photo ops, and a delightful donation ceremony to a worthy local charity that someone in the company has personal affection for.


It’s at this moment when a dealership becomes something of a community hub merged with a prom dance. But just like the new car smell, it disappears as quickly as it arrives.


*******


“I drove around the lot, and I don’t see an old Lincoln or a Ford Ranger anywhere, dude. Why aren’t you at my grand opening?” exclaimed John Miner in an early morning text message.


John is my buddy, a friend to all car enthusiasts, and the regional market manager CarCountry. So I candidly replied, “Bro I wasn’t invit… *never mind, I will see you there* .”


CarCountry in the year 2026 is much larger than it was in 2017, as smart fiscal planning ensured the company could buy more stores and build them up bigger and bolder. Our headcount also went way up, to the point where the Reputation Manager is no longer needed on the ground to ensure a smooth opening ceremony. These days I get photos via email for just about every event, with messages asking that I “put this on Facebook.” They mean everywhere from Facebook to Apple Maps, but I get the message.


I went home to change into a suit, gassed up my Lincoln Mark VIII, and engaged in the two-hour-long drive to CarCountry’s latest grand opening ceremony: a new Hyundai/Genesis facility for a well-regarded dealership in a swanky suburb. When I arrived, there was no parking near the showroom, so I drove to the back lot. As the curvaceous Mark VIII slinked into a lot of new Hyundais, its angry tubular headers echoed against a row of blocky 2027 Santa Fes. That’s always fun for me, but I noticed the showroom was darn near at the horizon when I parked.


“What the heck is going on here?” I openly exclaimed as I hustled into what was now a visitor parking lot for a one-night event that appeared to be the toast of the town.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


This grand opening was insane by my humble standards. Hyundai isn’t supposed to be a brand worthy of a high-budget celebration, but decades separate this brand from the more hardscrabble days of the Excel hatchback and Scoupe coupe. There were red carpets, multiple DJs, Korean-themed beverages and light bites, a radio station, a local news crew, and at least two city council members in attendance.


And this wasn’t even a celebration of the Genesis dealership, as that was being constructed a few meters away out of the shell of a former CarCountry Acura dealership. Not to bag on Honda’s premium automobiles too much, but you know things aren’t great when CarCountry repurposes your flagship dealership for a Genesis store, forcing them into the hole that once sold Genesis vehicles. And that hole used to be a Saab dealership in the 2000s. *Oh dear* , *how time marches on* .


Let’s get back to the festival of South Korean auto retailing, as it were. Never before have I seen a Hyundai dealership turn into a disco, but the party took a quick turn for me when I discovered that it wasn’t just fresh drywall, paint, and glass going up at this CarCountry store: The Reputation Manager learned that this store was using AI for significant parts of the sales process.


After sifting through the crowd, I met John and thanked him for the invite. Turns out he’s been mentoring everyone in the dealership, and he’s the driver behind its AI integration. *So this is why he wanted me here.* He eagerly forwarded me a recording of an AI chatbot and a customer. The person was looking at a used Kia K5 we had in inventory, and he loved the AI service enough to make a big deal about it to CarCountry management. I know car salespeople are hated in our society, but can AI really be that much better?


I listened to the entire call when I got home, and was flabbergasted. The chatbot did everything a salesperson does on the phone, but in less time and with fewer words. The customer spoke clearly, but rushed when saying his Latin-derived name. The chatbot nailed the pronunciation and successfully scheduled a test drive. The customer had a seamless purchase from there, using CarCountry’s online purchasing tool and even negotiated a few hundred bucks off the deal.


I was pleasantly surprised by the outcome. It was the first real-world scenario I’d seen of what’s likely to be the future of sales at a dealership, in the spirit of “tech companies” like[Tesla](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/tesla/) and[Carvana](https://www.hagerty.com/media/advice/piston-slap/piston-slap-carvanas-nation-of-automotive-irony/) . But unlike those media darlings, CarCountry’s formula possessed the ability to haggle with a real person before pushing a button to sign your life away complete a financing contract and receive the keys.


Not that consumers must haggle to complete the deal, but they have the option if interested. The internet tells me people just want to buy online, but I see way too many folks who want a test drive and little haggle time in the real world. These buyers simply want an easier way to perform said actions.


While I am bullish on AI helping people buy cars, I am bearish on AI for service customers. As if by magic, a bad review that explains my concerns surfaced on the dealership’s Google page.


Google


While it’s great to see someone buy a car from us and remain in our service department’s ecosystem for a full five years, I’m not sure that AI is yet able to do a good job keeping the customer. The above is still an updated review that went from 5 to 3 stars. I doubt I am telling you any new information when I remark that service departments make the lion’s share of revenue for a dealership. AI might make a decent receptionist or sales consultant, but I doubt it can handle the passion/urgency of service customers paired with the complexity of modern automobiles as they depreciate.


By now I’ve gone through hundreds of thousands of customer reviews in my career in reputation management. The sales reviews are generally easy to stereotype into a handful of concerns, but you have no idea what someone is bringing into a service department of a full-line automaker’s dealership. It’s even worse these days with unique EV and ICE platforms, not to mention software glitches that are downright impossible to predict.


I talked to John about my concerns, and this review. He’s still an AI bull while I remain moderately bearish. The dude knows way more about the car business—he started out as a teenage lot porter without a driver’s license, and moved up the ranks to regional market manager. Maybe he knows something I do not, or he possesses that insatiable optimism commonly found in the world of automotive retail. But service advisors wear more hats than (most) sales folks. Cars are too darn complicated these days, and people just seem angrier in our post-pandemic society.


Even if the AI chatbot knows the technical differences between a CVT and an automatic, or all the latest software patches, it still can’t listen and empathize with someone who needs a working vehicle in our car-centric society. And for that reason, perhaps the Reputation Manager’s job is also safe from this revolution in automation.


*The Reputation Manager will return…hopefully!*
